story:
Everett sat in the big arena. Many people were there to watch soccer. The players began to move across the field. Everett watched the ball go back and forth.

At lunch time, Everett's mom opened his snack bag. A chocolate cookie was inside. Everett reached for it. His fingers felt slippery from the juice he drank. He touched the cookie by accident. Later, his little sister touched it too. Now there were two different marks on the chocolate. Everett looked at both marks. "My marks are different," he said. "Her marks are different too."

Alexander found the note taped to the washing machine on Tuesday morning, his mother's round, careful handwriting made wobblier by the cast on her wrist. "Darks cold, whites hot, half the soap you think you need." Below that, a second list: "My hair: shampoo twice a week, oil the ends. Your face: wash morning and night, the blue tube, not soap." He read it twice, feeling something between being trusted and being handed a job nobody had asked him whether he wanted.

His mother had slipped on the back steps carrying groceries, and for six weeks her right hand was a stranger to her. Alexander's father worked until seven, and his little brother, Ben, was ten and useless and loud about it. So the house's quiet machinery, the washing and the creams and the schedules his mother had kept without ever seeming to think, fell to Alexander, who had never once considered that a towel needed washing on any particular theory.

The first load he ruined, turning a white shirt of his father's a pale accident pink with a stray red sock. His mother laughed until she had to sit down, cradling the cast, and said not unkindly, "Check the pile like it's evidence, sweetheart. Every piece." The second load he checked, item by item, and it came out clean, and he stood there with his hands in the warm clothes feeling a small, ridiculous pride, as if he had passed a test no one had announced.

The coin came in because of the dishes. Alexander proposed it as a fairness measure, a two-minute flip after dinner to decide whose night it was, and Ben agreed with the enthusiasm of a boy who believed fortune loved him. For four nights the coin came up heads, which meant Alexander washed, and by the fifth night Ben was pacing the kitchen with the fervor of a preacher. "It has to be tails now," he said. "Four heads in a row. Tails is due. That's just how it works." He said it with such certainty that Alexander almost believed the coin was listening.

"It's fifty," Alexander said. "Same as last night. Same as always." Ben demanded proof, so they sat at the table with a notebook and flipped the coin a hundred times, Ben calling out results, Alexander tallying, and somewhere in the middle of the runs, the three heads here, the five tails there, Ben went quiet in the particular way he did when the world rearranged itself under him. Alexander recognized the feeling, because he'd had it that morning reading the label on the blue tube, which said to leave the wash on for sixty seconds, and he had stood at the bathroom sink counting one mississippi, two mississippi, discovering that a thing he'd done sloppily every day of his life had an actual method inside it. The streaks meant nothing, and the method meant everything, and he couldn't have said why the two insights felt like the same insight, only that they did.

What stayed uncertain was the routine itself, the parts no notebook could settle. On Thursday he couldn't tell whether his mother's hair was clean or just recently wet, and rather than guess he carried the oil and a comb to the couch where she sat with her feet tucked under her, and asked her to teach him. "You're reifying the schedule," she said, smiling as he worked the ends of her hair between his oiled fingers. "The schedule is just a picture of what usually works. Your hands will learn better questions than the list can ask." He liked that, and also distrusted it, because her list had saved his father's shirt and his own face, and he wasn't ready to believe the list was only a list.

He did believe the coin, though, and that was where the trouble came. Saturday night Ben lost the flip again, sixth loss in a row, and slammed out of the kitchen, and Alexander sat with the cold plates thinking that fairness and kindness were not the same thing and might not even point in the same direction. The coin was extrinsic, a thing outside both of them, neutral and blind, and that was exactly its virtue and exactly its limit. Nothing in the fifty percent could notice a ten-year-old on the edge of tears.

So he washed the dishes himself that night, without saying it was a gift, and left the coin on the counter. Sunday morning he found it in Ben's fist at breakfast, his brother flipping it against his thumb, softly, over and over, murmuring "come on, tails" with the stubborn hope of someone who had learned the odds and decided to negotiate with them anyway. Alexander buttered his toast and watched, and after a while he said, "You know it doesn't listen." Ben flipped the coin high, caught it, and slapped it onto the back of his hand.

Colton went to his friend Maya's house on Saturday. Maya had a new drum in the garage. "I want to play it," said Colton.

Maya showed him how. "First, hold the stick like this," she said. Colton held the drumstick tight. Next, he had to repeat what Maya did. She tapped the drum slowly. He tapped it slowly too. Then Maya went faster and faster. Colton's arm got tired, but he kept going. Last, they played together and made real music. The drum sounded so loud and happy.

"Again, again!" yelled Colton. They played the same song over and over. Colton's hands hurt a little, but he did not stop. When he finally put the stick down, he was sweaty and silly. Maya laughed. Colton laughed too.

"You learned so fast," said Maya. Colton smiled big. He could not wait to come back and play more drums tomorrow.

Gavin sat at the kitchen table with his science textbook open, staring at the chapter about atoms and molecules. His mom had promised to help him study, but first she asked him to do something unusual. "I need you to be my test subject," she said, smiling. "I'm teaching a high school chemistry class next semester, and I want to try something with you."

She handed him a blindfold and explained the plan. His dad would drive their old car in circles around the driveway while the car's alarm went off, making a loud siren sound. Gavin's job was to sit on the porch, wearing the blindfold, and point toward wherever he thought the car was heading. "You'll be testing whether you can hear which way something is moving," his mom said. "It's connected to chemistry and physics both." Gavin wasn't sure how that made sense, but he trusted his mom enough to put on the blindfold.

The alarm started, and Gavin heard the siren wailing. His dad must have been driving toward him because the sound seemed to get higher and sharper as it approached. Without thinking much about it, Gavin pointed straight ahead. Then the car passed him, and something strange happened. The siren's pitch dropped. It became lower, almost like it was sighing as the car moved away. Gavin spun around and pointed backward this time. His dad circled back, and again the sound grew higher as it came near.

After several rounds, Gavin took off the blindfold. His mom and dad were both grinning at him from the porch. "You got every single one right," his mom said. "You tracked the car perfectly without looking." Gavin felt proud, but he was also puzzled. How had he known? The car had made the same alarm sound the whole time, yet it sounded completely different depending on which direction it was moving.

That night, Gavin sat with his mom and asked her to explain. She told him it had to do with sound waves, which were like invisible ripples in the air. When the car moved toward him, the sound waves got squeezed together and made a higher pitch. When it moved away, the waves stretched out and made a lower pitch. "It's the same principle that helps chemists study molecules," she said. "They use sound and light waves to understand things too small to see." Gavin thought about that connection and felt a vigorous spark of curiosity.

The next morning, Gavin looked out his bedroom window and spotted the recycling truck heading down the street, its backup alarm beeping urgently. As it approached the corner, the beep seemed to climb higher. He watched it turn away, and the sound descended into a lower tone. His brain suddenly sent him a signal: he understood this now. He grabbed his science notebook and started sketching what was happening to the sound waves in the air, imagining them as tiny springs that compressed and then stretched.

Eva walked into Room 12 with her backpack on one shoulder and a paper kite under her arm. She had made the kite at home, and she wanted to fly it at recess on the very first day of school. The kite was red with a gold tail, but one corner was bent and torn from where her little brother had sat on it.

At her desk, Eva smoothed the kite flat and looked at the damage. The torn corner was supposed to be a sharp point. Now it flopped like a dog's ear. She frowned. If she flew it this way, the wind would push it sideways.

Her new deskmate, a boy named Omar, leaned over. "That corner looks bad," he said. "Can you fix it?"

"I have to figure out how much to cut," Eva said. She found a ruler and a protractor in her pencil case. First she measured the two good corners at the bottom of the kite. One was 60 degrees. The other was 70 degrees. Then she thought about what her teacher had said last year, that the three angles inside any triangle always add up to exactly 180 degrees. She turned the pencil over and did the math on the back of her spelling list. 60 plus 70 was 130. That meant the torn corner had to be 50 degrees, because 130 plus 50 made 180.

"You need a 50 degree corner," she told Omar. "That's less than a right angle. A right angle is 90, and a full turn is 360, so 50 is not even a quarter of the way around." She drew the corner with her protractor, cut along the line, and taped a scrap of red paper into the gap. The new corner included a double layer of tape so it would not tear again.

Omar clapped once. "Brilliant," he said. "But will it work?"

"We'll try it," Eva said. "If it doesn't, we'll fix it again." At recess, the wind caught the kite and it climbed straight up over the soccer field. The gold tail whipped behind it. Eva let out more string and watched her red kite turn in the sky, a small bright square against the clouds. Omar ran to keep up with her, shouting, "Best first day ever!"

Victor wanted to hit the ball in a real game. His coach gave him one clear rule with four steps. First, plant your feet. Next, turn your hips. Then, swing level. Last, watch the ball all the way to the bat.

Victor tried the steps at the sports field. He planted his feet. He turned his hips. He swung level. But he missed the ball every time. "Watch the ball," Coach said again. "Keep your eyes on it."

That night, Victor went to the bathroom to brush his teeth. The room was dark, so he brought a flashlight. He stood in front of the mirror. He clicked the light on, then off, then on again. He leaned close and stared. The black dot in the middle of his eye was small in the bright light. In the dark, it grew big and wide. "Wow," Victor whispered. "It changes!" He clicked the light off and on five more times just to watch. Could everyone's eyes do that? He wanted to ask everyone at school.

The next day Victor had been ill in the morning, but he felt fine by afternoon. He ran to the field. The team would add up the runs at the end, and the winner got a small prize, a shiny blue ribbon.

Victor stepped up to bat. He planted his feet. He turned his hips. He swung level. He watched the ball all the way in. Crack! The ball flew over the shortstop's head. Victor ran to first base, grinning from ear to ear.

He raised his helmet. "My eyes were wide open the whole way!"

Grace stood in the kitchen scrolling through her phone when her mom came home with two grocery bags, her face tighter than usual. "Everything's more expensive," her mom said, setting the bags down harder than necessary. "I'm spending thirty percent more than I did last month."

Grace barely looked up. She had heard her parents worry about money before, the usual background noise of adult life. But then her Uncle Derek called that evening, and his voice on the speaker sounded different, excited in a way she hadn't heard in months. "The export numbers came through," he said. "Orders from overseas just jumped. The new machinery we're selling is moving fast." Uncle Derek ran a small manufacturing company that sold industrial parts to buyers around the world.

The next morning at breakfast, Grace asked her mom about it. "If Uncle Derek's stuff is selling better, why do you look worried?" Her mom explained that the country's currency had weakened recently. "That means when I buy things from other countries, I have to pay more dollars to get them. But it also means other countries can buy American goods cheaper now. Derek's benefiting from that." Grace nodded, thinking she understood, though something felt incomplete in the explanation.

That afternoon, she found herself testing the idea in her head. If foreign goods cost more, wouldn't people just buy less of them? She opened her laptop and looked at her family's planned trip to Canada next summer. She pulled up the hotel prices they had been considering and cross-referenced them with emails from her mom. The cost had jumped by two thousand dollars since her parents had started planning in March. "That's the currency thing," she realized aloud. Then she thought about Uncle Derek's machinery, sitting in a warehouse in Ohio. To someone in Germany or Japan, those machines probably looked cheaper now. They could afford to buy more of them.

Grace called her uncle that evening. "Are your customers buying more because you're cheaper now?" she asked. "That's exactly it," he said, sounding pleased that she had figured it out. "I've gotten orders from three new companies overseas this month alone."

She found her mom in the living room and explained what she had worked out. "So Uncle Derek is doing well because things cost him less to sell abroad, and you're doing worse because we have to pay more for the stuff we want to import." Her mom nodded slowly. "That's right. It's not fair to either of us, but that's how it works." Grace sat with that thought, understanding now that the world's apparatus of trade didn't care about any one person's vacation fund. Still, she felt something shift. Her disappointment about the trip mattered, but so did her uncle's relief at finally having steady work. She couldn't have both.

"Can we do the trip later?" she asked. "When the currency bounces back?" Her mom smiled, and Grace saw the tension in her face ease for the first time in days.

Declan was at the library on a brisk Saturday morning when he spotted something strange on the nature table. A burned pinecone sat next to a regular green one, and he couldn't stop staring at it. The burned cone was dark and crusty, while the green one was tightly sealed. He picked both up, turning them over in his hands. Why would someone leave a burned cone here?

He checked the schedule on the library bulletin board and saw that Ms. Chen, the librarian, was giving a talk about forests in ten minutes. Declan decided to ask her about the cones. While he waited, he looked at a book about wildfires and found a photo of a forest that had burned completely. The trees were black sticks against gray sky. But then the photo showed the same place one year later, and Declan's eyes went wide. The ground was covered with thousands of tiny green seedlings, like a carpet of babies had grown overnight. How did all those seeds get there if the fire destroyed everything?

When Ms. Chen arrived, Declan held up both cones. "This burned one has the seeds out," he said, "but this green one is totally sealed up. Did the fire crack it open?" Ms. Chen smiled and handed him a magnifying glass. He looked closer at the burned cone and saw empty chambers where seeds had been. Then he looked at the sealed green cone and felt along its closed edges. They were stuck together with something sticky and hard. "Heat does open them," Ms. Chen said, "but you figured out the interesting part. One kind of pine keeps its seeds locked away until the fire comes."

Declan set the cones down slowly, understanding flooding through him. The sealed cone wasn't waiting for any old heat. It was waiting for a wildfire. The burned forest in that photo didn't have seeds because the fire had destroyed them. It had seedlings because the heat had cracked open cones just like this one, releasing thousands of seeds onto the freshly cleared ground. He picked up the burned cone again, feeling its rough surface, and wondered how many of those tiny seedlings had grown from seeds that had been trapped inside, waiting.

Parker arrived at school early enough to watch the parking lot fill, which meant he had time to worry about whether arriving early was the kind of thing that marked you as earnest or just desperate. He sat on the curb with his phone—a flat rectangle that fit in his pocket and cost less than a textbook—and scrolled through pictures of his elementary school best friend who had moved to Portland and now made sourdough bread. The morning was already turgid with August heat, the kind that made the asphalt shimmer.

His new guidance counselor had assigned him to first period Advanced History with Mr. Reeves, a teacher who looked like he had been designed in a lab to frustrate seventeen-year-olds. On the syllabus, which Parker had printed out like a child, Mr. Reeves had written a single sentence: "You will learn to think like historians, not like people absorbing content." Parker had no idea what this meant, but it sounded ominous.

When he walked into the classroom, maybe fifteen other students were already there, and Mr. Reeves was writing on the whiteboard in letters so large and careless that they looked like a revisionist biography of the alphabet. The teacher turned around and told everyone to pair up and take a seat. Parker found himself next to a girl named Sasha who had the expression of someone who had already decided this year would be disappointing but was willing to be surprised.

"First assignment," Mr. Reeves announced, holding up two objects: an old brick of a phone with a stubby antenna and a photograph. "This is a Motorola prototype from 1973. The first mobile phone call was made on this exact model, which weighed about 1.1 kilograms. Ten years later, consumer versions sold for nearly 4,000 dollars." He set the photo down and tapped the ancient phone. "I want you to imagine buying this. Not wanting it. Buying it. You have maybe five minutes with your partner."

Sasha looked at Parker. Parker looked at the phone.

"Like, who would pay that much for a phone?" Sasha said, which seemed like an obvious observation, and Parker almost said so, but then he thought about his own phone, which did everything except make him breakfast, and he realized that saying "who would pay that much" was exactly the kind of thinking Mr. Reeves probably wanted them to litigate. So instead he said, "What did it even do besides call people?"

"Make calls," Sasha said flatly. Then her eyes changed. "Oh. Wait. Just calls? No texting, no apps, no internet, you just like, called someone?"

"And they had to be near a phone to answer," Parker added, warming to this. "Or you just got a busy signal, I guess. You had to know where someone was going to be."

Sasha leaned back in her chair. "That's actually insane. Like, how did anyone coordinate anything? How did you say 'meet me at the mall' if you couldn't text them five minutes before you showed up?"

Parker thought about this—really thought about it, the way his brain felt when he was reading a book that mattered. He thought about his grandmother talking about planning dates a week in advance because there was no way to change plans. He thought about the weight of it: 1.1 kilograms in your pocket, just to maybe reach someone. And the price, nearly 4,000 dollars, which meant only certain people had it, which meant something about power and access that felt different when he thought about it that way instead of just dismissing it as expensive.

"I think," Parker said slowly, "that maybe it wasn't actually the phone that people were paying for. I think they were paying for... like, the ability to be reached. Or to reach out from anywhere." He paused. "But that's kind of weird, because now everyone can do that and we all hate it."

Sasha grinned. "Yeah, now it's just torture. You can always be found."

Mr. Reeves was watching them from his desk, and Parker realized that this—this confusion and this thinking and this disagreement about whether something was good or bad depending on what angle you looked at it—might have been the whole point all along.

Alexander kept the tally sheet folded inside his seminar folder, and every Tuesday he added a mark to it. The seminar met in Room 114 after lunch, twelve students arranged in a circle of desks, and each week two of them argued a question while the rest took notes. Ms. Rivera only said whether the argument had held together, never what anyone should think. Alexander's sheet tracked something else: who had scored highest on the practice debate the previous week and where they landed the next.

The pattern had been bothering him for a month. Priya had topped the circle twice in September, then drifted to the middle. Marcus had gone last, nearly last, and then climbed to fourth. Alexander had a theory that Ms. Rivera's comments were causing it, that praise made people lazy and criticism made them work, and he had started to immerse himself in the numbers to prove it. He liked proving things. It felt like an aptitude finally finding its use.

The problem was Dewey. Marcus's partner in the third week had been a quiet boy named Dewey, who had scored worst in the circle, been scolded in front of everyone, and then jumped to fifth. Marcus had scored worst the week after, said nothing about it, and improved anyway, without the scolding. Alexander sat with that during the Tuesday when Priya and Elodie argued about whether school should start later.

"Your first premise only holds if buses run on the same schedule," Elodie said, leaning forward. "If the start time moves, the buses move, so the cost moves too. You've built your whole case on a condition you haven't checked."

Priya paused, and Alexander watched her do something he recognized: she changed one thing in her head. If the buses move, she said, then the district eats the cost, and if the district eats the cost, it cuts something else, so which program would you cut? Elodie had to answer, and her answer was weaker, and the circle shifted toward Priya. One change, and the whole argument tilted. Alexander wrote a single word in his margin: if.

After the seminar, he stayed behind to arrange the desks the way Ms. Rivera liked, which gave him time to think without anyone watching. He opened his tally sheet on the desk and looked down the columns. The highest scorers fell. The lowest rose. Even the ones who stayed exactly the same in effort, like Dewey, who admitted he hadn't practiced at all, had drifted toward the middle. Alexander tried his old theory one more time, the scolding theory, and watched it fail: the students who improved had nothing in common except where they had started, at the bottom.

He tried it as a conditional, the way Priya had. If the scolding caused the improvement, then the people who improved should all have been scolded. They weren't. Marcus hadn't been. If nothing caused it, then the scores should be random, and they weren't either; they moved inward, toward ordinary, every single time. He sat with that until the room got quiet enough to hear the radiator ticking. Whatever was true didn't live in Ms. Rivera's comments. It lived in the scores themselves. Extremes one week, middles the next, over and over, like water finding a level.

He found Marcus at his locker the next morning. "Do you remember when you scored last and then went up?" Alexander asked. "Did you do anything different?"

"I played video games all weekend," Marcus said, shutting his locker. "Why?"

"No reason," Alexander said, but he was already planning. Next Tuesday he would write his argument as a chain of ifs, the way Prieya did, and he would pick a topic nobody could scold him about either way. If he scored at the very top this week, he expected to fall after, and if he scored at the bottom, he expected to rise, and if his sheet was right, neither would mean anything about him at all.

At home that night he added two more marks to the columns, then filled the stagnant water glass on his desk with fresh water from the kitchen tap and carried it back to his room. He set it beside the tally sheet, took out a pencil, and began his outline with the words: If we agree that.

Aubrey was baking cookies at school today. Mrs. Chen said Aubrey could help. They mixed flour and butter together. Then they made cookie shapes.

Aubrey made round cookies. She made square cookies too. Mrs. Chen put them on a cold tray. Into the oven they went.

While they baked, Mrs. Chen brought out toy wagon wheels. One wagon had round wheels. One wagon had square wheels with corners. "Let's roll them," Mrs. Chen said. Aubrey pushed the round wheel wagon. It went zip across the floor so fast. Then Aubrey pushed the square wheel wagon. Bump, bump, bump. It stopped and stopped again.

"Why?" asked Aubrey. Mrs. Chen smiled. "Look at your cookies when they come out."

The cookies were ready. Aubrey's round cookies looked perfect. They sat flat and smooth. Her square cookies with corners had bumpy, broken edges. "Oh," said Aubrey. "Round is better. Corners make things bump." Mrs. Chen gave Aubrey a warm cookie. "You figured it out," she said.

Eli's phone buzzed on the kitchen table, and the message glowed up at him in letters the size of a hostage note: WHERE ARE YOUR GLOVES, YOU HERBIVORE?

He knew three things instantly. His older sister, Juno, only typed in all caps when she was standing outside in the cold. "Herbivore" was her favorite insult, because he ate everything on his plate like some kind of plant-munching dinosaur. And Mom was going to hear the phone buzzing and ask questions, which was the last thing he wanted, because the message meant Juno was locked out and Mom had banned the two of them from locking doors after the infamous Bathroom Incident of March.

He grabbed the phone with his gloves still on and swiped to answer. Nothing. He swiped again, harder, pressing so hard his thumb went white behind the wool. The screen ignored him like a cat pretending not to hear its name.

"Juno, hang on," he said out loud, then realized she couldn't hear him, which felt like the least useful sentence of his life.

He jabbed at the green button. He used a knuckle. He tried the corner of his sleeve, and then, in a moment of pure desperation, he grabbed a pencil off the counter and tapped with the eraser, as if the phone might mistake it for a finger and feel sorry for him. The screen stayed dark and smug.

Then he remembered something from a video he'd half watched while eating cereal, something about screens caring about electricity in your fingertip, not how hard you pushed. That was why they ignored plastic pens and ordinary gloves. His brain lit up like a vending machine. The gloves were the problem. The gloves had been the problem the whole time, and he had been standing here fighting a screen with a pencil like a cave man.

He yanked off a glove with his teeth, tapped the green button, and the call connected on the first try.

"Eli! It is negative one hundred degrees out here!" Juno's voice was so loud he had to pull the phone away from his ear, which meant her private rage was now being broadcast to the entire kitchen.

He heard Mom's chair scrape in the living room. "Who's at the door?"

"Nobody!" he called back, then lowered his voice to a whisper. "Back porch. The latch sticks, kick it near the hinge, it's more robust there."

"I'm going to inherit this house one day," Juno grumbled through the phone, "and I'm going to replace every door on it."

"Sure you are. Hurry up before Mom counts heads."

He shoved the phone in his pocket, dropped his glove, picked it up, and slid across the kitchen floor just as the back door banged open and a snow-covered sister blew in like a very angry blizzard.

Raphael wanted to make a race car out of a box. He found markers and tape at home. First, he drew big wheels on the sides. Next, he painted flames on the front. Then he taped a paper helmet to wear inside his box car.

Raphael pushed his car across the kitchen floor. It went fast! But then he noticed something. The back of the refrigerator felt very warm when he touched it. The front of the refrigerator was cold. He wondered why. He rolled his box car behind the fridge to see better. The heat from the back made his helmet too hot, so he took it off.

Raphael moved his car back to the cool kitchen. He realized the fridge was pumping the heat out and making it come out the back. That was the correct way it worked. He parked his race car in front of the fridge where it stayed nice and cold. Perfect for a racing champion.

Colton went to Ben's house to learn a song on the drum. Ben's drum was big and red. But there was a problem. A fat gray stone sat right where the drum should go. "That stone is as big as a hippo," said Colton. Colton pushed the stone. He grunted and puffed. The stone did not move one bit.

Ben ran to the garage. He came back with a long stick. First, they pushed a small rock under one end of the stick. Next, they tucked the other end under the big stone. Then, Colton pushed down on the long end with all his weight. The stone popped up like popcorn. "Whoa!" said Colton. He slid his hands farther from the small rock and pushed again. It felt even easier. Last, the stone rolled away down a shallow ditch by the fence. "We are strong!" yelled Ben.

"Now can we play the song?" asked Colton. Ben nodded. First, they tapped one time. Next, they tapped two times fast. Then, Colton had to repeat the two fast taps. Last, they hit the drum one big boom!

Colton tapped, tapped, and boomed. He did it again and again. The drum went boom, boom, BOOM. From the house, Ben's mom called out, "Is that a drum, or did a giant fall down the stairs?" Colton laughed so hard he fell off his drum stool. He jumped right back up. "Again!" he said. "First one tap, then two fast, then boom!"

Nicholas walked into soccer practice on Tuesday afternoon, but something felt wrong. His team had won three games, yet nobody was getting along. Mia and Jayden argued about who should kick first. Carlos sat on the bench looking sad because Coach always picked the same players to start. Even the new girl, Priya, stood awkward and alone by the goal.

During water break, Nicholas noticed something. The fast players like Jayden were also the meanest to teammates. The kind players like Carlos hardly ever got a chance to play. He realized they needed both kinds of people, just like landmarks need both tall buildings and wide open spaces. "What if we helped Coach make fair teams?" Nicholas asked Mia and Jayden. "We could pick players so everyone gets a real turn to play and everyone gets nice teammates." It took some talking to persuade them, but Jayden nodded. Mia said, "That's actually cool."

On Thursday, Coach listened to their idea. During the scrimmage, something amazing happened. When little Priya kicked the ball toward the goal, the whole team cheered equally loud, whether it went in or not. Jayden high-fived Carlos. Even though Carlos's kick missed, Mia said, "You almost had it. Great try." By the end of practice, everyone was laughing together, moving as one team instead of separate kids fighting for spots. Nicholas grinned as Jayden called out, "Same team again next practice?"

Colton had volunteered to build the ofrenda for the school's Día de los Muertos celebration before he fully understood what he was signing up for. His abuela had agreed to teach him, which meant Sunday afternoons in her kitchen, copying her diagrams onto a napkin while she stirred mole. There were rules he hadn't expected: the four elements of water, wind, fire, and earth, the arch of marigolds, the photos of the dead facing outward. He'd assumed it was decoration. It was closer to engineering.

"Wind goes where?" Abuela quizzed him on Thursday, hovering at the edge of the auditorium where the student committee was assembling tables.

"Papel picado," Colton said, pointing at the tissue-paper banners he'd spent two evenings cutting. "The cutouts flutter, and the wind moves through them. That's how the dead find their way."

She patted his arm twice, which he'd learned was her highest grade.

The problem arrived on Friday, in the form of a folded piece of paper slipped into his locker. Mr. Reyes, the biology teacher, had offered extra credit to anyone who could connect the cultural fair to real science, and Colton's lab partner, Priya, had signed them both up for a short presentation before the evening's ceremony. "You're already doing the ofrenda," she'd reasoned. "Just say something about marigolds and ecosystems. Ten minutes, tops."

Colton knew almost nothing about ecosystems. What he knew was the ofrenda, and he was starting to panic about that, too, because Abuela had to work the night of the fair, which meant he would set the whole thing up alone, in public, where everyone could watch him get it wrong.

He tried to suppress the dread and failed. That Saturday, he sat in the school library with three books about rainforest soils spread in front of him, looking for anything he could say that sounded intelligent. Most of it slid past him. Then he found a diagram in his abuelo's old science magazine, the one he'd brought from home because the library's rainforest section was pitiful. A rainforest scientist had traced the nutrients the forest needed to a desert an entire ocean away. Winds carried millions of tons of dust from the Sahara across the Atlantic every year, and the dust contained phosphorus that fertilized the Amazon, whose own soils were poor in that nutrient.

He read it twice, then laughed out loud and got shushed by the librarian.

The dead finding their way from far away. Things carried on the wind to a place that couldn't feed itself. It wasn't the same thing, exactly, but it rhymed in a way he couldn't stop thinking about, and it gave him his ten minutes.

Sunday, Abuela quizzed him again, and he got bold. "What if I moved the water glass to the far edge," he asked, "so the candles light the photos better?"

He wasn't serious; he was testing her. If she shrugged, then the rules were looser than they seemed, and he could stop worrying about every centimeter. She didn't shrug. She walked him to the window, where wind rattled the frame, and asked him what the dust on the sill would do if she opened it. "It comes in from wherever the wind has been," she said. "It lands where it lands because the wind put it there. You don't move the landing place to suit yourself." Then she added, almost kindly, "Ask me again next year. Asking is good. This year, do it as I showed you."

He did it as she showed her. On the night of the fair, his hands shook as he set out the salt, the bread, the little pan de muerto he'd baked himself, lopsided and slightly burnt. He arranged the marigold petals in a path from the auditorium door to the table, and Priya stood beside him while he explained to a scattered audience of students and parents that the paper banners existed because wind was how travelers found home. Then he told them about the dust, crossing an ocean to feed a forest that couldn't feed itself, and watched a woman in the front row nod slowly, as if he'd said something true.

After the crowd thinned, the janitor, Mr. Okafor, stopped in front of the ofrenda. "My mother would have liked this," he said. "She kept a lavish altar back home. Yours isn't bad for a first try." He straightened one of the papel picado banners that had gone crooked in the draft, and Colton found himself saying, before he could stop, "Next year I'm doing it again. I already know what I'd change."

Mr. Okafor smiled. "That's the whole point, isn't it?"

The wind stirred the cut paper above them, and Colton watched it flutter over the marigolds.

Thomas had been saving for three months to buy the new gaming laptop everyone at debate club kept talking about, and he was almost there, almost to the twelve hundred dollars he needed, when Marcus showed him something that changed everything.

They were sitting in the library after the debate team's practice, and Marcus pulled out a sleek credit card, black with silver lettering, holding it between his fingers like it was a prize he'd won. "My parents said I could get one for emergencies," Marcus said, grinning. "But look, if I use it now for the laptop, I can pay them back with my allowance. It's basically free money until I pay it off."

Thomas felt his stomach drop. He'd been working shifts at his uncle's coffee shop on weekends, doing yard work, skipping the movies with everyone else. The idea that Marcus could just buy the thing right now made him oscillate between anger and envy. That night, Thomas couldn't stop thinking about it. Why wait six more weeks when he could get it today? His parents said no to borrowing money, but what if he got a job that paid more? What if he asked for an advance on his allowance? The thoughts kept circling.

By the next Saturday, Thomas had convinced himself. He went to the bank after school and applied for a credit card. The woman behind the counter seemed surprised he was only fourteen, but his parents cosigned, and suddenly he had a card in his pocket. The laptop appeared on his doorstep four days later, and for exactly forty-eight hours, Thomas felt like he'd figured out something everyone else was still learning.

Then the first bill came. Thomas opened the statement expecting to owe around twelve hundred dollars. The actual number made him sit down hard on his bed: the laptop cost twelve hundred, sure, but there was an additional charge of sixty dollars in interest, and the card company was suggesting he pay only twenty-five dollars a month. Twenty-five dollars seemed reasonable, even generous. Thomas did the math in his head and decided he could manage it.

What Thomas didn't calculate was what happened after month two. The torrential list of charges kept growing, and when he actually sat down with a calculator at debate club one afternoon, his hands started shaking. If he paid only twenty-five dollars a month on his twelve hundred dollar balance, the chart on the credit card website showed it would take five and a half years to clear it. Five and a half years. He would be almost twenty years old before he owned that laptop, and by then it would be ancient. He scrolled further and saw the number that made him feel sick: over six hundred dollars in interest alone.

Marcus found him staring at the screen, still in the library. "You okay?" Marcus asked, sitting down beside him. Thomas didn't answer at first. Then he looked at his friend and said, "How much did your laptop actually end up costing?"

Mason wanted to build a tall tower out of straws for his sister's birthday party. He gathered long, thin straws from the kitchen drawer. His mom said he could use them to make something fun.

First, Mason made a square from four straws taped together. He stood it up on the table. When he pushed on one side, the square bent and squashed flat like a diamond. It would not stand tall. Next, Mason tried using three straws to make a triangle. He taped them together at each corner. When he pushed hard on the triangle, nothing happened. The triangle stayed strong and did not change shape at all.

Mason smiled. He knew what to do now. He built the tower one triangle at a time, stacking them up, up, up. First a triangle. Next another triangle on top of it. Then another one. Last, one more triangle at the very top. The tower grew tall and strong.

Mason placed his tower in the middle of the party table. His sister looked at it with wide eyes. "How did you make it so tall?" she asked. Mason did not say anything. He just pushed gently on the side of his tower. It did not squash. It did not fall. It stayed tall and straight, strong and still, ready for the party to begin.

His sister reached out and touched one of the triangles. "It is like magic," she whispered.

Luca spread the ledger pages across the playroom floor, where the afternoon light slanted through the window in a way that made the ink easier to read. His uncle had asked him to check the numbers in the community center's donation accounts, a task that seemed straightforward enough until Luca noticed something that made him pause. The columns of figures from the official books didn't match the ones from the backup records his uncle kept in a drawer, and worse, they didn't feel right when he scanned them, though he couldn't articulate why.

He began copying the donation amounts into his own notebook, arranging them in columns by how many times each opening digit appeared. It was an impetuous decision, born more from frustration than any clear method, but something about the distribution of numbers bothered him. In the official ledger, the digit seven appeared seventeen times at the start of entries. The digit nine appeared fourteen times. The digit one appeared only twelve times. When he counted the backup records, the pattern reversed. Ones dominated the first position, appearing in nearly a third of all entries, while nines and sevens together made up less than ten percent.

Luca sat back on his heels, staring at the two lists. His uncle had always been generous, honest in his way, but the donation records had been troubled for months. People complained that their gifts weren't being credited properly. His uncle insisted the system was just disorganized, that he would fix it eventually. Yet here on the playroom floor was a pattern that seemed to obfuscate rather than clarify. One set of numbers looked manufactured, spread across the digits too evenly, while the other had a natural lopsidedness to it. Luca's mind went to the most obvious explanation: someone had falsified the official records.

He heard his uncle's car pull into the driveway and felt his chest tighten. Part of him wanted to assume there was another explanation, that these papers represented different years or different categories of donations, something innocent he hadn't understood. His uncle had always helped him with math homework, had taken him to the science fair three years running. But Luca also knew that fortitude sometimes meant sitting with uncomfortable truths rather than looking away from them.

He gathered the papers carefully and went downstairs. His uncle was in the kitchen, setting down his briefcase with the tired gesture of someone who'd had a long day. Luca showed him the two sets of numbers and the lists he'd made, laid them out on the kitchen table without preamble.

"These are the same donations?" his uncle asked, his voice steady but something flickering behind his eyes.

"No," Luca said. "Official records and the backup you have upstairs. I noticed the digits that start each amount looked different."

His uncle studied the columns for a long moment. He didn't try to explain it away or offer excuses. "I see," he said finally. "The backup is the real record. I've been adjusting the official one because I used some of the donations for... other expenses. I was planning to replace it."

Luca looked at the evidence on the table. He understood now what it showed and what it couldn't show. The pattern in the numbers proved that one set had been altered to look random. But it didn't prove his uncle was a bad person, didn't reveal his desperation or justify it. The numbers could show him what had happened but not why, and knowing the difference between those two things felt important.

"We should tell the board," Luca said quietly, and his uncle nodded, as if he'd been waiting to hear someone else say it first.

Alicia arrived at Maya's house just as the basketball game tipped off, carrying her notebook and a bag of chips she'd promised to bring. Maya's little brother Ben was already sprawled on the carpet in his pajamas, even though it was only eight thirty. The three of them had a tradition: every playoff game, they kept score, argued about calls, and ate too many chips.

Halfway through the second quarter, Maya's phone buzzed. She read the message and groaned. "It's the student council group chat. The vote on moving the first bell to eight forty-five is Thursday, and I'm supposed to give a speech for our side." She flopped backward onto the couch. "I have nothing. Everyone keeps saying teens are just lazy, and I can't prove they're wrong."

"Lazy," Alicia repeated, and narrowed her eyes at the screen. "Your brother goes to bed at like eight thirty, right? And he's up at dawn?" Ben, without lifting his head from the carpet, said, "I woke up at six today. I watched cartoons before anybody else was even up." Alicia scribbled that in her notebook. "But you, Maya, and me, we could sleep until noon on a Saturday if nobody woke us. That's not the same thing. That's a pattern."

"A pattern of laziness," Maya said, but she sat up, which Alicia took as a good sign.

Alicia flipped back through her notebook pages. She had been tracking sleep for a science habit she'd started months ago and mostly abandoned, but the old entries were still there. "Look. In September I tried falling asleep at nine thirty, because my mom said little kids do it. I lay there for two hours. But over winter break, when I let myself stay up, I got sleepy around ten thirty or eleven, like clockwork, and I slept great." She tapped the page. "And Ben here gets sleepy right after dinner. Little kids and teens aren't on the same clock. It's not arbitrary. Something actually shifts."

Maya borrowed the notebook and read the entries herself, lips moving. "So the first bell at seven thirty is set for a body that wakes up early, but most of us don't wake up early anymore. That's the whole argument. That's it!" She started typing fast, then stopped. "But my data is one person. Yours. The debate guys will say that's just you."

"Then we test it," Alicia said. She proposed a plan: tonight, during the game, they would not force Ben to stay up, and they would watch what happened to their own sleepiness during the late game. If the pattern held, they'd get sleepy around the same time, teen bodies doing teen things, while Ben conked out early no matter how loud the arena crowd got on TV.

The game went into the fourth quarter, tied. Maya kept glancing at the clock, and at ten forty she yawned so wide her jaw cracked. "There it is," she said, almost gleeful, and wrote the time down. Ben had been asleep since nine, curled up next to the dog, having missed an entire quarter. Maya texted three friends and asked what time they'd fallen asleep last night: ten fifteen, eleven, ten fifty. She had five data points now, and she spent the commercial breaks drafting her speech, reading bits aloud. "Our reputation for laziness is a myth," she recounted, "and here are actual times from actual students."

Alicia pointed at the screen as the winning shot went in at the buzzer, and both of them screamed and woke the dog, and Ben, who blinked around at the bright living room with no idea what he'd missed. Maya looked at her speech, then at her friend. "Same time tomorrow? I want to test two more people before Thursday."

Mason's mom was ill. She was resting on the mattress in the quiet room. So Mason had a plan. He would bake her cookies.

Dad helped him start. First, they mixed the butter and sugar. Next, Mason cracked in two eggs. Then he poured the flour, slow as snow. Last, they scooped little rounds onto the tray. Dad slid the tray into the oven. The oven gave a soft hiss, like it was saying hello.

While the cookies baked, Mason had an idea. He would make Mom a little cookie house. He used long pretzel sticks for the walls. Four sticks made a square. But when he set it up, the square squashed. It slid down into a flat diamond shape. Mason tried again. The square squashed again. Again and again, down it went.

Then he tried three sticks instead. Three sticks made a triangle. He set it on the tray, and it stood. He touched it. It did not move. It did not squash at all. Mason made more triangles. He put one beside another. They all stood, strong and still. Dad looked over and smiled.

Mason built a little roof from triangles. He set a round cookie inside for a bed. The oven hiss faded, and Dad pulled out the tray. The cookies smelled warm and sweet. Mason let them cool, then piled them on a plate. He carried the plate and the pretzel house to the quiet room.

Mom sat up on the mattress and hugged him. She bit into a cookie and closed her eyes. "This is just what I needed," she said. Mason pointed at the little roof. "The triangles hold it up," he said. Mom took another cookie and said, "Then it is the best roof in the house."

Beatrice sat on the grass with her mom nearby. Her tummy made a loud growling sound. She wondered what that noise was. "Did you hear that?" she asked. Her mom smiled and said, "Your tummy is hungry." Beatrice played on the blue blanket for a while. Then her tummy growled again, even louder. It squeezed and moved inside her middle. The squeezing made air move around, and that made the sound. Beatrice giggled. "My tummy is talking to me," she said. "It wants food." Mom opened a snack bag. Beatrice ate some crackers. Soon her tummy was quiet and happy again. "My tummy tells me when I need to eat," Beatrice said. Mom hugged her close. "That's right. Always listen to your body and tell a grown-up nearby when you need something."

Alexis wanted to be the fastest runner at school. Every day after school, he played soccer and raced his friends. He did not want to sleep. He wanted to play all night and get faster and faster.

One week, Alexis stayed up late every single night. He played video games. He read books. He did not sleep much at all. Then came the big race on Friday. Alexis felt slow. His legs felt heavy. He could not run fast. His friend Maya ran past him like a purr of wind. Alexis came in last.

That night, Alexis's mom said, "You need nine to twelve hours of sleep every night. Your body does most of its growing while you sleep. The chemical that makes you grow is mostly released at night." Alexis did not believe her, but he was so tired that he fell asleep right away.

The next week, Alexis made a rule. First, he would eat dinner. Next, he would do his homework. Then, he would play for one hour. Last, he would sleep nine hours every night. He followed his rule every single day. When the next race came, Alexis ran faster than ever before. He passed Maya. He passed everyone. He crossed the finish line first and pumped his fist into the air.

Grace had claimed the table by the window in the library's back corner, the one with the afternoon light, and spread her materials across it: a bone folder, a stack of blue and cream paper, the half-finished zine she had been folding all week. The spreads needed a colophon, a small designed page at the back, and she was cutting a window into the card stock so a scrap of maps could show through when her friend Priya dropped into the opposite chair and slid her phone across the table.

"You have to look at this," Priya said. The screen showed a post from the school's anonymous confessions account, the kind that moved through the halls faster than any announcement. It claimed that the new visual arts intensive, the competitive program that had chosen its members last month, had admitted boys at a higher rate than girls. Someone had counted the numbers from the list posted outside the main office. Someone had done division.

Grace set down her knife. She had applied to the intensive herself and been rejected, and she had assumed, until this moment, that her portfolio simply had not been strong enough. "What are the actual numbers," she said, not quite a question, and Priya scrolled: forty-nine applicants, and the overall rate for boys was indeed higher, the poster had done that arithmetic correctly, which was more than most people did.

"It's Mr. Aldous," Priya said. "He runs it. He's always talking about the boys' portfolios in class." That was one explanation, a biased selector, and it fit what Grace half remembered: the way he would extol a certain kind of dramatic charcoal work, the kind more boys in their grade happened to do. But there was another possibility, quieter, that she had learned about somewhere and never expected to use, a thing that had happened once at a famous university, where an overall gap had hidden what happened inside each department. She could not remember where she had read it, only that the overall number had reversed when you looked at the parts.

"We can't know from this," Grace said slowly, and reached for a pad of sticky notes. "The overall rate depends on who applied to what." The intensive, she explained while drawing boxes, was actually four studios: drawing, ceramics, film, and design, and you applied to one. If the numbers weren't sorted by studio, the total could point one way while almost every studio pointed the other way. Priya frowned, so Grace took the practical route, the pragmatism of someone who would rather count than argue, and copied the acceptance list off the office door during the last ten minutes of lunch.

Back at the table, the light had gone amber, and the two of them made a grid on the back of a misprinted colophon, sorting every name into its studio. Within drawing, within ceramics, within film, the girls had been admitted at similar or higher rates than the boys. In three of the four studios the girls had actually done better. Only design, where nearly everyone was rejected, tilted the other way, and by less than the post had implied. Yet the girls had applied in greater numbers to design, the studio that turned away almost everybody, and that, not any selector's preference, was what the overall number had been measuring all along.

Priya sat back. "So the post is wrong." Grace trimmed the window in her colophon with a single clean stroke and held it up against the window, the streetlight showing through the cream paper like a small moon.

"Not wrong exactly. Wrong about what it proves," Grace said. "The total is real. But it can't tell us what happened, because it assumes the applicants were one pool instead of four." She thought of Mr. Aldoss again, his enthusiasm for dramatic charcoal, and conceded that the evidence could not clear him either. A selector could still prefer certain work and be saved by the arithmetic, or be entirely fair and look guilty of it; the sorted numbers answered one question and left a different one standing. She had been rejected from ceramics, where the girls had done well, and that was now a fact she had to carry without a story attached to it.

Priya began typing a reply to the post, drafting something conciliatory about how the numbers were more complicated than they looked, and Grace slid the map scrap behind the window in the colophon, pressing the fold flat with the bone folder, once, then again, until the paper held.

"Do we post the grid?" Priya asked, thumb hovering over send.

Grace looked at the grid, the four boxes with their small honest tallies, then at her finished page. "Post the grid," she said, and handed her the pen.

Tristan's fingers found the opening chord of the Hendrix riff he'd been working on for three weeks, and the studio monitor threw the sound back at him so crisp he could almost see it. Marcus, who owned the place and had enough expertise to know when someone was faking, nodded from behind the glass. They'd been at this since four o'clock, and it was nearly seven now, but Tristan's uncle's guitar—the one supposedly brought back from Vietnam in 1969—finally sounded the way it was supposed to.

"That's it," Marcus said through the talkback, his voice crackling like it was traveling through water. "That's the take."

Tristan set the guitar down carefully, the way his uncle had taught him, though his uncle had also been vague about where the instrument actually came from. Family legend placed it in Saigon, purchased from a street vendor by a young soldier who knew music and risk. Tristan had never questioned this. He'd simply inherited the story along with the faded brown case and the weight of something supposedly important.

Marcus emerged from the booth with two paper cups of coffee, the fastidious way he held them—one in each hand, level, not sloshing—suggesting he'd done this ten thousand times. "Your uncle play that thing for fifty years and never get it recorded?"

"He played it. Just never in a studio like this." Tristan accepted the cup, though he didn't really drink coffee. "He died last month."

"Ah. I'm sorry." Marcus sat on the stool beside him, and they both looked at the guitar. "Beautiful instrument. You thinking of selling?"

"No. I want to keep playing it. But I was wondering..." Tristan paused, unsure how to ask without sounding ridiculous. "Do you ever wonder if old guitars have a kind of signature in the sound? Like, if it's really old, it just sounds different?"

Marcus sipped his coffee. "What makes you think it's really old?"

"The story. Saigon, 1969."

"Your uncle tell you that?"

"Not in those exact words. But yeah, that's what the family says." Tristan looked at the guitar more carefully now, at the wear pattern on the neck, the way the finish had faded unevenly. "I figured, if it survived that long, the wood would have matured or something. Changed. That's supposed to matter with guitars."

Marcus set his cup down on the windowsill. "What if I told you there's a way to check if the wood is actually from 1969?"

Tristan felt something shift in his chest. "Like how?"

"Carbon dating. Not the kind they use on fossils. The kind that works on once-living material like wood. You can date back to about fifty thousand years before the carbon in it gets too degraded to read. The half-life is about fifty-seven hundred years, so anything from the last few decades is pretty precise." Marcus tilted his head. "There's a lab two hours from here that does it. They drill a tiny hole, take a sample. Doesn't hurt the guitar."

Over the next two weeks, Tristan went back and forth about whether to do it. His uncle's words kept surfacing in his memory: "This guitar has a story." But which story? The family version, burnished by decades of telling, or whatever the wood itself might say? He acquiesce to the idea that he needed to know. He made the appointment.

The results came back on a Tuesday afternoon, an email with a PDF attachment. The spruce in the top of the guitar dated to 1962, plus or minus two years. Not 1969. The back and sides were older—1954. Someone had built this guitar in 1962 or 1963, not purchased it from a street vendor in wartime.

Tristan sat with the guitar in his lap and thought about his uncle, who had taken the family's assumption and never corrected it, perhaps had believed it himself or had believed something else entirely. The evidence showed when the wood had stopped living, when the carbon in it had begun its long, slow decay. What it couldn't show was why his uncle had told the story the way he had, or what truth he'd been protecting or inventing.

He played the opening chord again, and this time he listened not for signatures of age but for his uncle's hands in his own fingers.

Maika sat at the library table with her survey in front of her, tapping her pencil against her chin. She and three other eighth graders had spent the past week asking people at the mall whether the school should extend lunch period from thirty to forty minutes. Out of the fifty-two people they'd surveyed, forty-one said yes. That was about 79 percent, which seemed like a clear answer, and Maika felt certain she could walk into Principal Chen's office and make her case.

"Wait," said Devon, leaning over to look at her clipboard. "You asked fifty-two people. That's it?"

"We were there for four hours," Maika said, a little defensive. "Do you know how many people we had to approach before someone would actually stop and talk to us?"

"Yeah, but fifty-two people out of how many? Like, there are over a thousand kids in this school."

Maika frowned. "We didn't need to ask everyone. That's the whole point of a sample."

"A dubious sample, maybe," Devon said, and she wasn't trying to be mean about it. "My older brother has to do this statistics thing in high school. He said asking only fifty people is basically useless."

That gnawed at Maika as she sat in the library after school that Thursday. She pulled up a website on the public computer, searching for something about how many people you actually need to ask. The article she found mentioned margin of error and confidence levels, words that swam past her brain without sticking. But then she found a different source that stated something clearly: a properly random sample of about 1,000 people gives a margin of error of about plus or minus 3 percentage points, whether the population is a city or a nation of hundreds of millions. What matters is the sample size and how randomly it was chosen, not the population size.

She read it twice. The example used a nation of hundreds of millions, and it still needed 1,000 people. That made 50 seem impossibly small. But then something else caught her attention. The article said what matters is how randomly the sample is chosen. Maika's group had only asked people at the mall on a Saturday afternoon. Not random at all. Those people probably had more leisure time, more money for lunch, different reasons to care about school altogether.

She texted Devon: "Want to do this again but actually right?"

By the following Tuesday, they had expanded their group to eight people and divided the school into sections. Some surveyed during lunch in the cafeteria. Others caught students in the hallway between classes. A few went to the morning study session where quieter kids hung out. When Maika tallied the results two weeks later, the number had shifted. About 64 percent still wanted the longer lunch, but it wasn't the overwhelming majority she'd imagined. Several students actually preferred the current schedule because it meant an earlier end to the school day.

Maika printed out her new results and made an appointment with Principal Chen, bringing both sets of numbers. "The first survey was just fifty people in one place," Maika explained, pointing. "This one is 847 people across the whole school, and I asked them at different times and different places."

Principal Chen looked from one paper to the other, then smiled at Maika. "I appreciate you thinking this through so carefully."

The studio smelled like burnt coffee and old carpet, and Tristan had been playing the same eight bars for forty minutes, which was the point, or so Derek the engineer kept insisting. "Once more, clean take, no ghost notes," Derek said, leaning toward his fastidious wall of faders as though the guitar itself might misbehave. Tristan's guitar had belonged to his great-grandfather, or that was the family version: a parlor guitar, honey-dark, with a rosette of tiny inlaid stars, supposedly carried over from the old country in a steamer trunk. His grandmother called it the brother guitar because she said it had been passed between two brothers who never spoke to each other again, and Tristan had grown up on the story the way other kids grew up on bedtime songs.

He played the eight bars again, and this time the take was clean, and Derek gave him a thumbs-up through the glass. "That wood," Derek said afterward, when Tristan was coiling cables, "I don't know. It sounds older than it looks." Tristan said it was older than everybody, actually, maybe a hundred years, and Derek shrugged and said his cousin worked at a lab that did dating on old instruments for insurance appraisals, and if Tristan ever wanted to know, a little sample from an invisible spot inside the sound hole would settle it. "Settle what?" Tristan asked, and Derek said, "Whatever stories you've got attached to it."

Tristan's grandmother did not exactly forbid it. She said she preferred the story to the verdict, which Tristan thought was a strange thing for a woman who watched courtroom shows every afternoon and shouted "follow the evidence" at the television. He went anyway, because the guitar was insured under her name and she had signed the form, sighing, refusing to argue, the way she acquiesced to his haircut and his playlist and most things that were not worth her remaining energy.

The lab report came back on a Tuesday, and Tristan read it twice on the bus. The wood, the report said, was from a once-living sample, and the result put it at roughly eight hundred years old. Eight hundred. He checked the sheet for a typo, some missing decimal, because eight hundred was not older than the family, it was older than the country the family had supposedly carried it from. He looked up why such a test could reach so far and found that it worked on once-living material like bone, wood or cloth, and was useful back to roughly 50,000 years, because carbon-14 had a half-life of about 5,730 years and too little remained beyond that. So the guitar sat comfortably within range. The number was not a mistake.

He now had two competing explanations. One: the story was true, and the lab was wrong, which would mean the whole method was wrong, which would also mean every other thing dated that way was wrong, and that seemed like a lot of collateral damage to save one family legend. Two: the story was not exactly false but borrowed, an old guitar acquired somewhere along the way and folded into the steamer trunk story because the trunk story was better. Behind the first explanation, he noticed, sat an assumption he had never questioned: that because the guitar was genuinely old, the family's story about its age must be true. The test could date the wood. It could not date the telling.

His grandmother listened with her hands folded, then said, "Eight hundred years," and was quiet for a while, and then she laughed, which was not what he expected. "So your great-grandfather bought an antique," she said. "That vain old peacock. He let us think he hauled it across an ocean on his back." She wiped her eyes. "He probably got it at an estate sale and kept his mouth shut."

The following weekend Tristan was back in the studio, and Derek asked, through the talkback mic, whether the mystery had been solved. "Half of it," Tristan said. "The guitar's older than the story. The story's mine now, I guess." Derek grinned and said that was how most songs worked anyway. Tristan set the eight-hundred-year-old wood on his knee, and the little inlaid stars caught the booth light, and he counted them in.

Gavin had been staring at the same page of his chemistry book for ten minutes. Atoms were supposed to be everywhere, in the air, in his desk, in his own hands, but no matter how hard he looked at his palm, he saw nothing but skin and a Band-Aid he'd forgotten to take off. "How am I supposed to study something invisible?" he muttered.

His little sister Maya wandered in holding a plastic tub. "Can we do the secret listener game? Pax said he can tell which way a car is going with his eyes closed, and I bet he's lying."

Gavin closed the book. "Fine, but only for ten minutes." He tore a paper towel into a strip and folded it into a blindfold. The driveway ran along the side of the house, and from the front porch you could hear every car on Maple Street. Maya sat on the steps, blindfolded, while Gavin wrote "toward" or "away" on his tablet for each car that passed. She got six out of ten wrong and yanked the blindfold off in disgust.

"It's not fair, they all just get loud then quiet," she said.

Gavin started to agree, then stopped. Pax wasn't the smartest kid in class, but he wasn't a liar either. He cupped his hands over his ears, thinking. When the ice cream truck came up the street every summer, the song sounded one way coming and a different way going. High, then it slid down low. That was a thing you could hear without seeing anything at all.

"New rule," he said, grinning. "Don't listen to loud and quiet. Listen to the pitch, whether it sounds high or low. Try one more." He blindfolded her again, and this time he gave a vigorous thumbs-up to Mrs. Okafor's gardeners across the street, who waved back like they did this every day. A pickup rolled toward them and Maya shouted "Toward!" before it even passed the house. The next one, a delivery van fading down the block, dropped low and long, and she called "Away!" She got eight in a row.

"That's your signal," Gavin said, tapping her blindfold like it was a medal. "Pax wasn't lying."

Mayay beamed, then squinted at the chemistry book still open on the porch rail. "Is your homework about invisible stuff too?"

"Yeah. Little tiny pieces of everything, too small to see."

Maya considered this, kicking her sneakers against the step. "So how do you know they're real?"

Gavin looked at the street, where a distant car was rising toward them, its sound climbing up and up like it was on its way somewhere small and hidden. "You test it," he said. "Like the cars." He picked up his pencil and, for the first time all afternoon, started writing. "Maybe I can dissolve salt in water tomorrow and see what happens. If the pieces are really in there, the water should taste like it." Maya leaned over his shoulder and whispered, "I get to stir."

Theodore stared at the math test on his desk and felt his stomach rumble. He had been thinking hard for the past forty minutes, working through word problems and fractions, and now his brain felt like it was made of fog. He looked at the clock. Just ten more minutes before lunch, and he was absolutely starving.

By the time Mrs. Chen collected the papers, Theodore's head was pounding and his concentration had completely disappeared. He could barely think about anything except food. At lunch, he devoured his sandwich in three bites and was still hungry for more. His best friend Marcus laughed at him. "You ate like you hadn't eaten in a week," Marcus said. Theodore shrugged. He had no idea why the test made him so hungry when he had eaten the same breakfast as always.

That evening, Theodore was reading a book about how the human body works when he found something mysterious. The book said the brain uses about twenty percent of the body's energy even though it is only about two percent of its weight. He read it twice to make sure he understood. That meant his small brain was using as much energy as his arms, legs, and stomach all combined.

Theodore sat up in his chair. His brain had been working super hard during the test, using way more energy than usual. That was why he was so hungry. It was not just an excuse. His brain had actually burned through his fuel trying to solve all those problems. He grabbed a pencil and started to arrange the facts in his notebook, drawing lines to show how his brain's energy use connected to his hunger after the test. Finally, the mysterious feeling made sense.

The note taped to the tank said to move Comet before cleaning, because the glass cleaner was corrosive and would burn the fish's gills. Declan read the citation at the bottom of the care sheet twice, some science journal he'd never heard of, and wondered what a magazine about fish knew that he didn't. Maya stood beside him at the kitchen counter with the net. "You cook, you catch," she said. "I already boiled the noodles. I'm on dinner strike."

"I'm not on strike," Declan said. "I'm learning." He had come over to make garlic butter pasta, following Maya's grandmother's recipe card step by step, and the butter had gone from solid to golden to fragrant while he practiced with the whisk. Then they'd spotted the tank, cloudy and green, and the chores had multiplied.

He lowered the net and swept it through the water where Comet gleamed, an orange flicker near the surface. The net closed on nothing. He tried again, slower, aiming exactly at the fish, and missed again, and Comet didn't even seem startled. "It's like he's not there," Declan muttered. He crouched until his eyes were level with the water and watched how the gravel at the bottom seemed to bend where it met the surface. Was the fish bending too? He raised the net and held it above the water, staring down. Comet looked closer to the top than the plants around him suggested he should. Maybe the fish only looked shallow. Maybe he was really deeper.

On the next try, Declan swept the net below where Comet appeared to be, into empty-looking water, and the fish dropped into the mesh with a soft whoosh. He grinned so wide his cheeks hurt. They set Comet in a mixing bowl of tank water, cleaned the glass, and returned him to his home. Then Declan finished the pasta, twirled a forkful, and tasted the garlic butter he'd made himself. "Okay," Maya said, pulling up a chair. "You're officially off my boycott list."

Florence went to the store with Mom. She wanted to find a toy elephant. They walked down the long aisles together.

"Excuse me," Florence said to a store helper. "Where are the toys, please?" The helper smiled. "Thank you for asking so nicely," she said. "The toys are over there." Florence ran to find them.

She looked at the shelves. Toys were everywhere. Some were messy and mixed up. Florence found a blue elephant! But it was on a high shelf. She could not reach it.

"Will you help me, please?" Florence asked the helper again. The helper came over. She reached up high and brought the elephant down. "Good asking for help," the helper said. Florence held the elephant tight and smiled.

Marcus had been stocking shelves at the grocery store for three weeks when his coworker Devon brought up the diamond ring.

They were in the back room during the afternoon lull, breaking down cardboard boxes for recycling. Devon held up his phone, showing Marcus a photo of a massive stone set in white gold. "My girlfriend's birthday," Devon said. "Two months' salary, they told me at the jeweler. That's the rule, apparently. That's how you know it's real love." Devon sounded impetuous, already convinced, but he was also asking something without quite asking it. He made minimum wage, same as Marcus.

"Two months is a lot," Marcus said. He folded a box carefully at its creases, thinking about the numbers. Two months meant most of Devon's paychecks gone. "What's it actually for? Like, what does a diamond do?"

Devon laughed, but there was a defensive edge in it. "It doesn't do anything. It's beautiful. It's supposed to last forever. It means something."

Marcus didn't argue because he could see the distinction Devon was making and wasn't sure Devon was wrong. He went home that night, though, and thought about it. His older sister had taken a philosophy elective and left her textbooks around. He found something about value and necessity, about how things cost money not because of how much you need them but because of how scarce they are compared to the demand. He read a section twice, the words seeming to move around on the page.

The next Saturday, Marcus was working the register when Mrs. Chen came in with her grandson. They bought a few groceries, nothing much, and when Mrs. Chen got to the water, she bought six bottles instead of her usual two. The boy looked thirsty, worn out from the summer heat. She was being careful with money but bought extra water anyway. Marcus rang it up and didn't think much of it until she mentioned they'd been hiking that morning and had underestimated how much fluid they'd need.

That afternoon, during his break, Marcus found himself online, reading about a stranded hiker who'd been rescued after three days in the desert. The article mentioned that toward the end, the man would have traded anything he owned. His watch, his wallet, his grandmother's ring that he was carrying in his pack. He would have traded all of it for a bottle of water. Marcus stared at that sentence. It seemed to contradict something he'd been thinking, until he realized it might not.

When Devon came in Monday, Marcus caught him before the shift started. "I was thinking about the ring thing," Marcus said. "And I think there might be two different ways to see it that don't actually contradict each other." He explained what he'd been reading, slowly, trying to get the logic right. "Water is cheap because there's so much of it around. Like, if you're dying of thirst, water is worth everything. But most people aren't dying of thirst most of the time, so one more bottle of water isn't worth much to most people in most places. A diamond is expensive because almost nobody has one and everybody wants one, so each individual diamond is worth a lot." He stopped. "The ring isn't worth more than water because it's actually more useful. It's worth more because of how many people want it compared to how few there are."

Devon was quiet for a moment, folding his apron in his hands. "So when I buy it for her, I'm not buying something that's objectively worth two months of my work. I'm buying into something because everyone agrees it's valuable."

"I guess," Marcus said. "But that doesn't mean it's wrong to do it. You're just doing it with your eyes open about what's really happening."

Devon nodded slowly, then smiled. "That's actually way less romantic when you put it that way."

Raphael wanted to make a space helmet. He had one big rule for making things. First, look at a picture. Next, get all the stuff. Then, build it. Last, try it on. He found a picture in his space book. The helmet was round and white, with a little window.

He got a big box, tape, and silver paper. Then he cut a hole for his face. He taped the silver paper all around. Last, he put it on. He looked in the mirror. "That is not correct," he said. The window was on the side of his head. He could only see the wall.

Raphael tried again. This time he made the window in front, right where his eyes were. It fit just right. Now he was an astronaut. He began to race through the kitchen in his helmet. "Zoom! To the moon!" he said.

Then he saw something odd. His cat, Milo, was asleep behind the refrigerator. Raphael stopped. Wasn't that a cold place? He put his hand on the back of the fridge. It felt warm! How strange, he thought. A fridge should be cold, but the back was warm? Milo purred and did not wake up. Raphael petted him with one hand. Then he flew on, straight to the moon.

Isabelle stared at the line of code on the screen and realized she had no idea what was supposed to happen next. The community center's computer lab smelled like new equipment and the vending machine coffee someone had left on a desk that morning, and through the tall windows she could see people playing basketball on the outdoor court, which made her wonder briefly why she was inside typing words that meant nothing to her.
