The instructor, Marcus, had stepped away to help another student, so Isabelle was alone with the Python code that should have printed "Hello World" but instead kept throwing an error message she couldn't parse.

She had signed up for the coding workshop on a whim, mostly because her college applications asked what interested her beyond school, and she had already written about volleyball and debate club. Something about the promise of learning to build things, to make computers do exactly what you wanted, had pulled at her. The first session two weeks ago had enthrall her with the basic logic of it all: if this, then that; variables that held information like tiny containers; loops that repeated actions until they were done. She had felt the strange satisfaction of making a simple program that calculated compound interest, something previously opaque becoming transparent.

But now, halfway through week three, she was hitting a wall. Marcus returned and leaned in to look at her screen, then pointed silently at a missing quotation mark. "Ah," she said, feeling the small shame of the careless error. After she fixed it and the program ran, Marcus mentioned that they would be learning web development next week. "You know someone invented the entire web, right?" he said. "Tim Berners-Lee. Did it at this research place in the 1990s." Isabelle nodded as if this were obvious information she had simply forgotten. Marcus moved on to check on someone else's work.

The comment nagged at her through the drive home. She looked it up that night and fell down a research rabbit hole that kept her up past midnight. Berners-Lee had created the first web page in 1991, posted it at CERN. But what struck her was the part about 1993: the lab had released the underlying technology royalty-free, which meant anyone could use it without paying. She tried to imagine what that decision meant. If they had not done that, if the web had been locked behind licensing fees and corporate control, would it even exist the way it did? Would there be a Wikipedia, a YouTube, a million small blogs run by teenagers in their bedrooms? The mendacity of her own earlier assumption hit her suddenly: she had thought of coding and the internet as products someone had made and was selling, as closed systems you had to pay to enter. But it had not started that way.

At the next session, Marcus brought up web development and explained HTML, which turned out to be simpler than Python: just tags that told a browser how to display things. Isabelle wrote her first page in twenty minutes, a basic structure with a title and some text about why she wanted to learn this skill. As she looked at it rendered in the browser, she felt something shift. This was not just about syntax or logic anymore. Someone had invented this language, and then chosen to let it exist in the world for free, which meant she could learn it, could build things with it, could contribute to it later if she wanted. The generosity of that choice, whether conscious or not, had shaped everything that came after.

She stayed after class to ask Marcus more about Berners-Lee. Marcus explained that many people thought the web should have been a product, that its creator could have gotten rich. "Why didn't he?" Isabelle asked. Marcus shrugged. "Different era. Different values, maybe. He believed people should be able to access information." Isabelle thought about this framing, about the gap between what could have happened and what did. She understood the economic logic of selling something: you wanted to profit from your work, and that seemed basic, fair even. But she also saw the incipient world that would have existed if the web had been locked behind paywalls, more restricted, more controlled. There was something worth protecting in how it had actually turned out, even if she could not have explained exactly why.

On her way out, she stopped at her computer one more time and added a few more elements to her page: a list, some bold text, a link to another site. It was small and clumsy, but it was hers, and it was live on the internet, accessible to anyone who had a connection and the right URL. She saved the file and closed the laptop. Next week they would learn CSS, Marcus had said, and after that maybe JavaScript. She did not know yet what she would build with these tools, or whether she would keep going with this at college. But she knew now that the choice was not between using something free or paying for something closed. The choice existed because someone, decades ago, had decided that knowledge and creativity should flow freely through networks, and she was benefiting from that choice every time she sat down to code.

Connor stared at the computer screen in the community center's tech room, where Mr. Patel had left him with the syllabus for the afternoon's coding workshop. The assignment seemed straightforward: write a program that simulated a car crash response system. He had to create code that would detect a sudden change in speed and trigger a safety response, nothing more.

He started typing, fingers moving across the keyboard as he wrote his first version. The program would detect deceleration, then immediately trigger the airbag. Simple. He ran it, and on the screen, a small animation showed a car hitting a wall. A small circle appeared where the airbag should be. Connor sat back, satisfied. The system worked.

But something nagged at him. He thought about his uncle's car accident last year. His uncle had mentioned that the airbag had already deflated by the time he realized what was happening. Connor remembered being confused by that detail at the time, thinking the airbag should stay inflated to protect him throughout the crash. He wondered if his simulation was missing something irrelevant to the basic mechanics or actually important.

He decided to modify his code. Instead of having the airbag stay inflated, he added a second trigger that would deflate it thirty milliseconds after it inflated. He stared at the numbers on his screen for a moment, thinking about what that meant. A blink took much longer than that. He ran the simulation again.

The animation played. The car decelerated. The airbag appeared and disappeared so quickly that Connor almost missed it. He played it again, slower this time, watching frame by frame. The sensor detected the sudden deceleration, the airbag inflated, and then, before any visible crash impact had fully occurred on screen, it was already deflating through the vents he had added.

Connor leaned back and thought about his uncle again. His uncle had probably reached out to protect himself and found nothing there, because the bag was already releasing its cushioning and collapsing. The airbag wasn't designed to stay full. It was designed to absorb the impact quickly and then get out of the way. That made sense now. The speed wasn't irrelevant at all. Everything depended on those milliseconds.

He saved his revised program and titled it "Airbag Response v2" before logging off. As he gathered his things to leave the community center, he pulled out his phone and texted his uncle: "I finally understood how your airbag worked. It was already deflating when you felt the impact."

Luca had spread the drama club ledger across the playroom floor because it was the only room in the house where nobody asked questions, and right now he did not want questions. The ledger was real, printed from the treasurer's spreadsheet, three months of ticket and concession sales, and it smelled faintly of his little sister's crayons, which were still heaped in the corner where she had abandoned them mid-masterpiece. He was supposed to be building the model set for the fall play, a shoebox proscenium with painted flats, and instead he was cutting the numbers out of the ledger with a pair of safety scissors, sorting them into piles by their first digit.

"Dani," he said when she appeared in the doorway, holding a juice box. "Look at this. I made piles."

Dani knelt on the carpet, which she considered her territory, and poked the pile of clippings that began with 1. It was small. The pile that began with 9 was a mountain. "You made a mess," she said, "but an organized one."

"Exactly," Luca said. "An organized one. That's the problem." He had read, late one night, in the depths of a Wikipedia spiral, that in real collections of numbers, like populations or accounts, about 30 percent of entries start with 1 and fewer than 5 percent start with 9, and that when people invent numbers they spread the digits evenly because even feels honest. So he had tested it. Nineteen of the ledger's sixty-two entries began with 9. Six began with 1. Either Marcus, the co-treasurer and his oldest friend in the club, had invented most of the fall figures, or something else was going on, and Luca could not decide which, which was why the model set stood half-built and why the scissors kept moving.

He tried the first explanation on for size: Marcus faked it. It fit the piles. It fit the fact that Marcus had refused to hand over the spreadsheet itself and printed only the summary pages, a move that could be read as laziness or as a deliberate attempt to obfuscate. It even fit the fact that the fall fundraiser had supposedly raised four hundred dollars more than the bake-sale table could plausibly have earned. Luca felt the satisfying click of a story that explained everything, and because he was seventeen and impetuous, he had already drafted a message to the club advisor accusing Marcus by name. It sat unsent on his phone.

Dani read over his shoulder anyway, because sisters do that. "You're going to send that?" she said. "Based on paper piles?"

"Based on evidence," Luca said, but he heard how thin it came out, so he picked up a clipping and looked at it properly for the first time. Nine dollars. Another one. Nine dollars. Nineteen dollars, adult-and-child pair. He picked his way through the mountain of nines and found that nearly all of them were ticket prices, fixed at the door by vote of the whole club last spring. The digits hadn't been invented one by one; they'd been stamped out by a single decision made before any money changed hands. The piles told him nothing about Marcus at all, and the accusation message suddenly looked like something a different, worse version of Luca would send.

"So it's fine?" Dani said, peeling the straw off her juice box.

"It's not fine," Luca said slowly. "It's not-not-fine either. I don't know." He explained it to her by laying it out on the carpet, because explaining to a nine-year-old was the only reliable way to find out whether he understood something himself. "The digit thing catches people who make up numbers, right? Too many nines and sevens, too few ones, that's the fingerprint of a liar. But our ticket prices are nine dollars, so of course there are nines everywhere. That doesn't prove Marcus is honest. It just proves my test doesn't work here. A test that can't tell the difference between lying and a nine-dollar ticket can't tell me anything."

"So the piles are garbage," Dani said, and rolled one flat piece of paper under her palm.

"The piles are honest," Luca said. "I'm the one who was garbage. I assumed the numbers were the kind of numbers the rule works on, and they're not." He looked at the mountain of nines again, then at the small, suspicious excess in the bake-sale column, where the amounts did vary, where the rule might actually apply, and where the count was too small to mean anything either way. Six entries. You could not hang a friendship on six entries. He deleted the draft message, which took more fortitude than he would have admitted, and lay back on the carpet with his arms behind his head.

"There's still the four hundred extra dollars," Dani said, reasonably, from beside him.

"I know," Luca said. "I'm going to ask him. In person. Without accusing him of anything, just asking where the fundraiser numbers came from." He sat up, gathered the clippings into a shoebox, and set it beside the half-finished proscenium, whose painted flats were drying at exactly the angle his sister had knocked them into an hour ago. Then he texted Marcus three words: "come over tomorrow?" and, while he waited, picked up a brush and finished the back wall of the set in flat, unremarkable gray.

Florence went to the store with her dad. She wanted a toy lighthouse. She had seen one on a tall shelf. But it was too high up.

Florence bumped into a big pile of stuffed toys. They fell down. The pile made a messy heap on the floor. "Sorry," said Florence. She picked up a soft gray elephant and put it back. She picked up the rest, too. A shop lady came to help. "Please, can you bring the lighthouse down?" asked Florence. "I cannot reach it." The lady smiled and brought it down.

Florence hugged the lighthouse. "Thank you," she said. Then she saw a little boat toy next to it. A boy was playing with the boat. "Watch out," he said. "The lighthouse is calling my boat in."

Florence pressed the button. The light went on and off, round and round. The boy steered his boat away from the rocks. "Your boat went away because the light told it where the rocks are," said Florence. "The lighthouse is not calling it in."

The boy smiled and sailed his boat the other way. "Let's try again," he said. Florence pressed the button one more time. "Away goes the boat," she said.

Dylan walked into the art room at the community center. He saw a big art project on the table. There was a sparkly flag that needed to go up high on the wall.

"How do we get it way up there?" Dylan asked. His teacher showed him a wheel with a rope. She said, "Pull down on this end." Dylan pulled down hard on the rope. The sparkly flag went up, up, up to the top of the wall. He pulled again and again. Each time he pulled down, the flag went higher.

Dylan wanted to try it by himself. He found the rope in the basement where they kept supplies. He made his own flag from red paper. He tied it to the rope. Dylan took a calm breath. He pulled down on the rope slowly. His red flag rose up to the top of his poster board. He had done it.

"I made it work!" Dylan called out. His teacher came over and smiled. "You learned how the pulley works," she said. Dylan looked at his flag at the top. He pulled the rope down again just to see it rise one more time.

The mantis was supposed to be the centerpiece of Addison's portfolio for the county youth art show, a voracious predator rearing back with its forelegs raised, and at four inches tall, in the sketch Grandma had praised twice, it looked perfect. The trouble began when Addison decided that four inches was timid. She wanted it life-sized for a mantis, then a little more than life-sized, then, after watching a monster movie trailer on her phone in the kitchen, she wanted it enormous. "Big gets attention," she said, wedging the gray clay with the heel of her hand on the kitchen table while Grandma shelled peas on the porch outside the screen door.

Grandpa's basement held the good supplies: the armature wire, the wooden modeling tools worn smooth at the handles, the box of clay he had ordered online the week she arrived. He had been a high school art teacher for thirty-one years, but he had a policy, which he stated once and never repeated, that he would not tell her how to do anything until she had tried it wrong at least once. So he sat in the lawn chair by the dryer and read his newspaper and said nothing while she built.

Her first mantis stood six inches tall and held together beautifully. The joints, the taper of the abdomen, the triangular head with its bulging compound eyes, all of it worked. She photographed it from three angles, then rolled a mass of clay the size of a grapefruit and started again, this time at twelve inches, exactly double, using the small one sitting on the dryer as her reference.

The doubled mantis failed before she finished the second foreleg. The legs, which on the small version had been slender and elegant, sagged at the middle joints like wet noodles, and when she tried to lift the body to attach the thorax, the whole thing flattened onto the newspaper with a soft, horrible squelch. Grandpa turned a page of his paper. Addison stared at the ruin and then at the intact small mantis, comparing them side by side, because the legs were exactly the same shape. Nothing about the design had changed. Only the size had.

She got her phone and opened the calculator, because something was nagging at her, a half-remembered thing from a science video she had watched at two in night in February. She measured the small mantis's leg: three millimeters thick. The big one's was six. She multiplied the length by two and looked at what doubling did when you carried it through the other directions. The surface of the leg, its cross-section, its skin, went up by four. But the volume, the actual clay, the weight of it, went up by eight. She wrote 4 and 8 on the margin of the newspaper Grandpa had already finished, then checked it a second way with different measurements and got the same numbers. So the doubled leg was carrying eight times the weight on only four times the leg to carry it with. Of course it sagged. It wasn't her design that had failed. The design was fine at any size where the clay was thin enough to hold its own weight, and wrong at any size where it wasn't. She thought of the movie trailer again, the skyscraper-tall insect toppling a bridge, and felt a small, fierce satisfaction, as if she had caught the filmmakers in a lie.

There was a limitation, though, and she wanted to be honest about it. Her numbers told her why the big mantis had collapsed, but they couldn't tell her the best size to build at, or what pose would look the most alive, or whether the judges would care about any of it. The math was a floor to stand on, not a map. She would still have to guess, and guess again.

"So what happened?" Grandpa asked, folding the paper at last. He was looking at the flattened body on the table, but his voice had that quality she had learned to recognize, interest without verdict.

"Doubling the length makes the surface area four times bigger," she said, "but the weight eight times bigger. The legs couldn't hold it. That's why there aren't giant insects. That's why elephants have those thick legs and bugs can get away with toothpick legs." She rolled the failed clay back into a ball, working the air pockets out of it, because clay could always be reused, nothing about this attempt was wasted. "I'm building it again at nine inches. That's one and a half times, which puts the weight at about three and a half times and the legs at a little over two, so I thicken the legs past proportion and use wire inside them anyway."

Grandpa set down the paper, went to his supply shelf, and came back not with advice but with the spool of heavy armature wire and the good wooden tools, the ones with his initials burned into the handles. "The wire cutters are in the second drawer," he said. "Try it."

From the porch, Grandma called that the peas were done and there was lemonade, and Addison said in a minute, in a minute, already cutting the first length of wire.

Natalie stared at the Python error message on her screen, the cursor blinking in the darkness of the computer lab like a tiny heartbeat that refused to steady. It was midnight, and everyone else had left hours ago, but she couldn't let it go. The program was supposed to analyze her friends' social media activity, a project she had pitched to her Computer Science teacher because it seemed simple enough: pull data, sort it, visualize patterns. Instead, the code kept breaking in ways that made her feel like she was trying to read a language that refused translation.

She had decided to historicize her approach, breaking the problem into pieces like an archaeologist working backward through layers. First, she had written the basic function to connect to the API. That worked. Then she added the loop to collect follower counts and interaction data. That worked too. But when she tried to correlate follower numbers with actual communication frequency, the whole thing collapsed into incomprehensible errors. The logic seemed sound in her head. On screen, it was chaos.

Her phone buzzed. A text from her best friend Marcus: "Still up?" She didn't answer. Instead, she pulled up her own social media feeds and began scrolling through her own account as a test case. She had 847 followers. She opened her messages and started counting people she had actually had a real conversation with in the past month. The number came out to fourteen. She tried another angle: who would she actually call if she needed help moving? Six people, maybe seven if she was being generous. Her followers and her real relationships were in completely different categories, kept in separate boxes.

She started investigating other accounts, beginning with the school's popular kids. One girl named Sophia had 2,341 followers. Natalie opened her public messages and found them full of people trying to catch her attention, making jokes, asking for advice, tagging her in photos. But when Natalie looked at Sophia's actual activity—her genuine back-and-forth exchanges—there was a sullen quality to it, as though Sophia was performing closeness rather than experiencing it. Three people seemed to occupy most of her actual conversation time. Everyone else was audience.

Natalie's hands moved across the keyboard almost without thinking. Instead of trying to make her data correlate something that couldn't correlate, what if she just tried to show the gap itself? She wrote a new program, a simple one, that would display two numbers for each account: followers listed, and then a count of people who had exchanged messages more than once in thirty days. She ran it on a dozen accounts, including her own. The patterns emerged like a photograph developing in chemical solution.

The results were stark and strange. Her older brother, a software engineer working for a tech company, had often joked about his acolytes online, people who followed his advice and reposted his content. He had thousands of them. But when Natalie ran her program, his actual conversation network was smaller than hers. The gap between his audience and his real relationships was enormous.

She sat back in the chair, the realization settling into her like something heavy. The program worked now, and it was showing her something true. But she wasn't sure what to do with the truth. The gap wasn't a failure in her code. It was real. People could be deeply seen by a few while being seen by thousands, and those two kinds of seeing were not the same thing at all. She could show this to her teacher as a project that technically succeeded, and technically failed to prove what she had originally wanted to prove. Or she could let the code sit here in this lab, in the quiet of the night, and think about whether knowing something meant you had to explain it.

She closed her laptop and picked up her phone. There were three new messages from Marcus, each one shorter than the last.

The community center smelled like floor wax and old coffee, and the coding class met in the back room where the folding tables wobbled if you leaned on them too hard. Connor sat near the window because it was the only seat with a working outlet for his laptop. The syllabus taped to the wall said Week Three: Variables and Debugging, and underneath it someone had written in pencil, "bring snacks." Connor had not brought snacks. He had brought his uncle Marcus instead, sort of, because Uncle Marcus was sitting in the lobby waiting for his shift at the garage across the street, and he had come in early specifically to drop Connor off, which he never did.

The teacher, Ms. Okafor, gave them a broken program to fix. It was supposed to simulate a safety system: read a number for how fast something was slowing down, and if the number passed a threshold, print "deploy." Connor's program printed "deploy" even when he typed zero. He stared at the screen for a while, tapping the edge of the trackpad. His neighbor Priya kept glancing over, and he kept his shoulders hunched so she couldn't see his screen, because asking for help felt like admitting something.

He decided to do what Ms. Okafor had suggested in week one, even though at the time it had seemed irrelevant to him, a rule for little kids who couldn't read their own code. Change one thing, she had said, and only one thing, then run it again. He didn't believe it would help, but the alternative was sitting there until class ended. So he found the line with the comparison in it, the part that checked whether deceleration was greater than the threshold, and he flipped the greater-than sign to less-than. Just that. He ran it. Now it never printed "deploy," not even when he typed ninety-nine.

That was the moment something clicked, quiet and small. The sign was backwards, and it had been backwards the whole time. It wasn't broken in some mysterious deep way, the way he'd assumed for twenty minutes. He flipped it back to greater-than, typed zero, and the program stayed silent. He typed ninety-nine and "deploy" appeared. He sat back and let out a breath. Priya looked over. "Did you fix it?" she asked. "The sign was backwards," he said, and turned the laptop so she could see, because it turned out showing someone felt fine once the thing actually worked.

After class he found Uncle Marcus in the lobby, reading a car magazine with the pages bent back. "How was computer school," Uncle Marcus said, not looking up. "Good. Hey, the guy from that crash on Elm Street, the one who said his airbag was already flat when he got out?" Connor had overheard him complaining about it at the garage two weeks ago, convinced the thing had never fired at all. "That's normal," Connor said. "It inflates in about thirty milliseconds, faster than a blink, then it deflates through vents to cushion the impact. The sensor catches the sudden deceleration and triggers a small chemical charge that makes nitrogen gas." Uncle Marcus lowered the magazine a half inch and looked at him over the top of it. "It's gone before your eyes even finish closing," Connor said. "It did its job and quit." Uncle Marcus was quiet for a second, then he laughed, short and surprised. "So the guy's mad it worked." "Basically," Connor said, and closed his laptop bag. Uncle Marcus stood up, folded the magazine in half, and held the door open. "Come on, then. I'll buy you a soda and you can tell me what else they're instilling in you over there."

Eli stood in the kitchen on Saturday morning, staring at his phone like it had personally betrayed him. The group chat for the robotics team was blowing up, and he needed to reply right now, but his thumbs refused to cooperate. Every tap on the screen went ignored. Every swipe landed in the wrong place. It was as if his phone had decided to become a herbivore and only respond to plants.

"This is ridiculous," he muttered, jabbing at the keyboard icon again. Nothing happened. He'd inherited his older sister's impatience along with her bad habit of checking texts while eating, and right now both traits were making him want to throw the phone across the room. Instead, he looked down at his hands. Oh. Right. The winter gloves.

His mom had made him wear them to take out the recycling, and he'd been too lazy to remove them when he came back inside. Eli peeled off the thick gray gloves and tried typing again. His thumbs pressed the screen, and the keyboard popped right up like his phone suddenly remembered how to behave. He typed three quick messages, hit send, and felt that small surge of victory that came with solving something stupid on his own.

But then curiosity got weird. Eli put the gloves back on and tried to answer a call from his friend Marcus. The phone ignored his tap on the green button. He took one glove off, used just his bare left hand, and the call went through. "Hey," Marcus said. "Why did you take so long to answer?" Eli didn't explain. Instead, he hung up and experimented. Left glove on: nothing. Right glove on: nothing. Both gloves off: the phone responded so fast it was almost embarrassing. He'd been using touchscreens his whole life without really thinking about how they actually worked.

At dinner, Eli's mom asked why he kept taking his gloves on and off. "Just testing something," he said, which was technically true but also the most unhelpful answer possible. His little sister Zara rolled her eyes because she was eleven and that was apparently her main hobby now. She was robust in her opinions about everything, especially her brother's weirdness.

That night, Eli sat on his bed and thought about all the times he'd complained about his phone freezing in winter, all the times he'd tapped the screen at the bus stop and gotten frustrated. He'd always assumed the phone was just being broken and cold. But it wasn't the cold. It was the gloves. His fingertips could talk to the screen. The plastic and fabric couldn't. He picked up his phone and texted Marcus: "Why does your phone work with gloves but mine doesn't when they're on?" Marcus replied instantly with a bunch of question marks, followed by "?????? what are you talking about."

Eli grinned and typed back: "Never mind. I figured it out."
